The Ooldea dunnart (Sminthopsis ooldea) is a small dasyurid marsupial endemic to the arid and semi-arid regions of central and western Australia. Neonates of this species are exceptionally altricial, emerging from the birth canal after a brief gestation and weighing a mere 0.01 grams [Wwb = 0.01 grams] at birth. These tiny newborns must immediately crawl to the pouch and attach to a teat, where they will remain for a prolonged period of development. The total duration of gestation is 21 days [tg = 21 days] under typical maternal body temperatures, reported at approximately 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], which aligns with the short gestation lengths characteristic of other small dasyurids. This brief intrauterine phase is followed by an extensive period of lactation within the pouch, during which the young undergo most of their morphological differentiation. The low birth mass places the species among the smallest of marsupial neonates relative to adult size, a physiological necessity imposed by the limited energetic resources available during gestation.

Lactation proceeds for approximately 70 days [tx = approximately 70 days] after birth at a maintained body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], at which point the altricial neonate achieves nutritional independence. The weaning mass is recorded at 4.8 grams [Wwx = 4.8 grams], a value that reflects the substantial growth that occurs entirely within the pouch and during the early post-pouch period. At this stage, the young are fully furred, capable of thermoregulation, and able to consume solid food items such as small invertebrates. The transition from a completely milk-based diet to independent foraging represents a critical period of high mortality in wild populations. The weaning mass is modest compared to adult body size, indicating that considerable somatic growth must occur after nutritional independence. Field studies suggest that juveniles emerging from the pouch display a rapid increase in body mass, with adult dimensions attained several months after weaning as they continue to refine their hunting skills on a diet of ants, termites, and other arthropods.

Sexual maturity is reached at 300 days [tp = 300 days] after birth at a body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], a relatively delayed developmental milestone for a mammal of such diminutive size. This post-weaning period of immaturity allows for the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of reproduction in an unpredictable desert environment. The ultimate wet weight of adult individuals is approximately 11 grams [Wwi = approximately 11 grams], though field records indicate a range of 11 to 18 grams depending on seasonal conditions and resource availability. This adult mass is consistent with the lower end of dasyurid body sizes and confers several advantages, including reduced absolute metabolic costs and the ability to exploit small prey items. Males and females are similar in size, with no pronounced sexual dimorphism reported in the literature. The modest body weight of the Ooldea dunnart is an adaptation to its arid habitat, where energy and water conservation are paramount.

The maximum lifespan of the Ooldea dunnart in the wild has been estimated at approximately 4.9 years [am = approximately 4.9 years] under a typical body temperature regime of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], a remarkably long duration for such a small mammal. This extended longevity is unusual among the smallest dasyurids and may be linked to a slow metabolic rate or a life-history strategy that buffers against the high environmental stochasticity of arid zones. Basal metabolic rate measurements conducted via respirometry at a thermoneutral temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C] have yielded a value of 18.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 18.9 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively low metabolic rate likely contributes to the species' ability to persist in resource-poor landscapes by minimizing daily energy requirements. The combination of a small body size and a low mass-specific metabolic rate represents a key physiological adaptation to the extreme temperature fluctuations and sporadic food availability characteristic of the Australian interior.

Reproduction in the Ooldea dunnart is strictly seasonal, timed to coincide with the austral spring and summer when invertebrate prey is most abundant. Females typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with an average litter size of 8 pups [N_R_i = litter size of 8 pups], yielding an annual reproductive output that is moderate among small dasyurids. The maximum reproductive rate, measured under optimal captive conditions at a body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], supports these field observations of a single annual litter [F_R_i = single annual litter] containing 8 pups [N_R_i = containing 8 pups]. The relatively large litter size for such a small marsupial imposes a significant energetic burden on the lactating female, who must increase her food intake substantially to support the growth of the litter within the pouch. This reproductive strategy is balanced by the low birth mass and slow post-natal development, which together ensure that the female's metabolic demands are spread across an extended lactation period. Such a suite of life-history traits reflects a careful trade-off between offspring number, offspring size, and maternal survival in a harsh and unpredictable environment.
